chapter_theme: Courtesans (பொது மகளிர்): their love lasts as long as a man's money and turns hostile when it ends. The chapter blames the men who trust them as much as the women, calling them beasts, dupes and people whose bodies are full of sin.
structure_note: Two quatrains are the dupe's own speech: the death-pact abandoned at the cliff's edge (372) and the address to his own heart (376). The rest alternate between the women's mercenary love (371, 373, 374, 379) and the men who are fooled by it (375, 377, 378, 380).

371.reading: The lamp's light and the friendship of harlots, examined steadily, are no different: the light ends when the oil runs out, and their love ends when the hand is empty.
371.nuance: Mudaliar takes கை, the hand, as the money held in it.

372.reading: The woman with fine jewels said she would leap with us from the high peak; but at the peak, since we had no gold, she showed a pain in her feet, wept, and wouldn't come on.
372.nuance: The speaker is the dupe himself, and the promise he recalls is a lovers' death pact. Mudaliar takes the foot pain as a lie and the tears as feigned; the verse says only that she showed the pain and wept.

373.reading: Even if he were the red-eyed Mal whom the gods of the wide sky worship, women tender as plucked shoots would join their hands in worship and send away a man with nothing in his hand to give.
373.nuance: The joke lies in the gesture: hands joined as if in worship are the hands that dismiss him. Mudaliar takes மால் as Tirumal, with Indra as an alternative; Shanmuganar has Indra.

374.reading: To women with loveless hearts and lovely blue-lily eyes, men without money are poison; but even a man seen by all driving an oil press is sugar to them if he has earned wealth.
374.nuance: Mudaliar glosses the oil press as a low trade. The verse says money erases even that rank in their eyes.

375.reading: Like the eel that shows one end to the snake and the other to the fish in the clear, sweet pond, women of double conduct are embraced by the dull-witted, who are like beasts.
375.nuance: Mudaliar explains the eel's trick as matching each man's nature and showing him love. The verse turns part of the blame on the men, who are the beasts. Shanmuganar's commentary on this quatrain appears under 374.

376.reading: The woman of golden bangles who said 'we'll never part from you', like a gem strung on its thread and the anril birds that never separate, has turned away like a fighting ram's horn; my good heart, will you stay, or will you go?
376.nuance: The speaker turns from her to his own heart, which is still with her. Both commentators take the last line as 'will you stay with her or come with me?', so the heart is a separate party the man has to win back.

377.reading: Those who are fooled into thinking theirs the love of a worthless woman who licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from their hands, and then lies down like a balking ox, will be laughed at by many.
377.nuance: Mudaliar cites a belief that the wild cow's lick pleases at first and kills later. குப்புறூஉம் is either lying face down, as Mudaliar takes it first and Shanmuganar takes it, or bounding away, as in Pope.

378.reading: Those who mean to reach the right path won't embrace the large breasts of doe-eyed women who go their own way, women who seem kind while a man is infatuated and turn harsh as a ram's horn 'once they are full'; who is full is disputed.
378.nuance: Mudaliar glosses செந்நெறி as the path to liberation, which makes avoiding these women a renunciant's discipline; Shanmuganar has only 'the good way'.

positions.position: தாம் ஆர்ந்தபோது refers to the men: when, now poor, they come of their own desire, the women turn harsh.
It refers to the women: once they are filled with a man's wealth, they turn harsh.

379.reading: Some do take bright-browed women as their own, trusting words spoken to be believed by women who hide their harmful intent; but such women belong to no one except their own bodies.
379.nuance: Pope adds 'they have no souls to give'. Mudaliar's gloss is narrower: their attachment reaches only as far as their own bodies.

380.reading: The scheming of bright-browed women whose minds are with another man is clearly known, and still those whose bodies are full of sin don't grasp it; who it is that knows is disputed.

positions.position: The dupes themselves examine and know the guile, yet don't grasp that the women should be shunned.
The world knows the guile clearly; the sinful fools alone don't know it.

links.note: 911 says the sweet words of women who desire wealth, not the man, bring harm. 371 gives the mechanism: their love burns only while the money feeds it.
Both are the dupe's own speech recalling a vow of inseparable love, a death pact in 372 and a promise never to part in 376, broken when his money ran out.
912's women weigh the profit before they speak of their virtue; 374's women weigh only wealth, so the poor man is poison and the oil-presser with money is sugar.
920 names இருமனப் பெண்டிர், double-minded women, among the company of the ruined; 375's eel, showing one face to the snake and another to the fish, pictures the double mind.
Both use the fighting ram's horn, which twists away, for the courtesan's love turned to hostility.

918 says the embrace of deceiving women is an அணங்கு to those without discernment; 377's wild cow, whose lick pleases and then kills in Mudaliar's gloss, is the same danger, with public ridicule added.

914 says those who seek the wealth of grace won't touch the base charms of women who count only wealth; 378 says those who mean to reach the right path won't embrace them, which Mudaliar takes as the path to liberation.
913 compares the false embrace to holding a stranger's corpse in a dark room; 379 says the women belong to no one but their bodies. Both deny that anyone is present in the embrace.
917 says those without firmness of heart embrace women whose hearts are on other things; 380 says those full of sin don't grasp the guile of women whose minds are with another man.
